summary: Children measure area by covering a figure's interior with unit squares — no gaps or overlaps — and counting the covering squares systematically, stating the answer in square units (square cm, square m, square in, square ft). Work includes irregular and L-shaped figures (decomposed into rectangles), comparing two shapes by their counts, and telling the area (every covering square, including the squares along the inner edge) apart from the length of the boundary (unit lengths around the outline, i.e. perimeter) and from a count of only the border squares. Concrete tiles on a real surface precede squared-paper diagrams. Keep to whole unit squares at this stage, treating edge part-squares informally.
misconceptions: Counts the squares around the boundary (perimeter) instead of the squares covering the interior.
Leaves gaps or overlaps, or counts unsystematically so squares are missed or double-counted (especially on L-shapes).
Counts every partly-covered square at the edge as a whole square, overestimating.
Gives the count as a bare number without the square unit.

activities.title: Tile and count an L-shaped garden
steps: Cover an L-shaped figure's whole interior with unit squares so there are no gaps and no overlaps, including the awkward squares inside the notch of the L.
Count the covering squares systematically — row by row, or by splitting the L into two rectangles and counting each — marking each square as you count it so none is missed or double-counted.
State the result in square units, e.g. '18 square cm' or in square metres, not just a bare number.
Repeat with a plain rectangle and then compare two shapes side by side, deciding which covers more by comparing their counts.
activities.insight: Area is the count of unit squares that cover the inside of a shape — notches and all — and is about the surface inside, not the fence or distance running around the edge.

activities.title: Tile a real surface before squared paper
steps: Lay square-centimetre tiles across a small real surface such as a book cover, filling it with no gaps or overlaps; if strips narrower than a tile are left at the edges, note them informally as part-squares rather than counting them as whole tiles.
Count the tiles and say the area in square centimetres.
Then move to a squared-paper diagram of the same shape drawn at the same size (one paper square for each tile) and count the covering squares there.
activities.insight: Measuring area means physically covering a surface with equal square units and counting them; the squared-paper diagram is a picture of that same covering.

activities.title: Compare and check with quick counting questions
steps: Given two shapes on squared paper, decide which covers more area by counting each one's squares.

Answer a short set of count-the-squares questions using whole-square figures — a plain rectangle and an L-shape, each with a definite count — then separately look at one shape with part-squares at the edge and discuss (rather than score) how to handle the part-squares informally.

Watch for a tempting wrong answer that comes from counting only the border squares (or the unit lengths around the outline) instead of all the squares covering the inside, and explain why it is wrong.
activities.insight: Comparing areas means comparing counts of all the covering squares, edge squares included; counting only the border squares does not give the area, and the distance around the outline (perimeter) is a different thing from the area inside.

activities.title: Read a finished counted figure
steps: Study a figure already filled with unit squares and its revealed count, e.g. '18 square cm'.
Retrace which squares were counted and confirm every square inside the outline, including those along the edge, is counted exactly once, and nothing outside the outline is counted.
Say back how the count and unit were obtained.
activities.insight: A completed, correctly counted figure models what a finished area measurement looks like: every interior square counted once, with the square unit named.

checkQuestion: Give a few figures on squared paper — a plain rectangle, an L-shape, and one with part-squares at the edge — plus a book cover and square-centimetre tiles. Say: 'Find the area of each by counting.' Watch whether they count the covering squares or the boundary, whether they cover with no gaps/overlaps and count systematically, what they do with part-squares, and whether they state the unit.
checkAnswer: The child covers each interior with unit squares (no gaps or overlaps) and counts them systematically — decomposing the L-shape so every square is counted once — gives the count in square units (e.g. '18 square cm'), handles edge part-squares sensibly rather than as whole units, and compares two shapes by their counts.
